results.title: diff-tour: AI writes the code. Learn to read it like a senior engineer. | Product Hunt
results.content:
People rarely write code by hand anymore. AI often reviews it too, and software moves so fast that reading every line is hard. Still, I'm sure of one thing: understanding code matters as much as ever. And understanding code means learning how a senior engineer thinks. That is what lets you give AI the right instructions, notice what really matters in a problem, design well, and keep a project moving in the right direction.

So diff-tour teaches that thinking on real changes. Point it at a branch, and the AI coding CLI you already use writes a tour of the change. Then you step through it with → and ←:

   What the change is for, and which files to read next, including ones that didn't change [...] What a senior engineer asks: What if this runs twice? Can it be rolled back? Would the tests fail if the code broke?

   What must be fixed, what's only a nit, and what looks risky but is fine

   The moments they'd stop and say "wait", asked as questions so you can guess before you see the answer

Getting started is just this: install with the one-line script in the README, then run it in any git repository:

```
cd your-repo
tour
```

The first run asks for a language and an AI CLI, with recommended choices already selected. Press Enter three times and the tour starts being written.

Things I cared about:

   It's read-only. The AI gets a copy of the files git tracks and read-only tools, enforced by command-line flags, not only by the prompt [...] , what must be fixed and what is a nit, and where they'd say "wait", asked as questions so you guess first. Runs on your AI coding CLI. Read-only, open source.

results.title: AI Wrote ‘Perfect’ Code. My Senior Dev Rejected It. Here’s Why He Was Right.
results.content:
AI doesn’t think about what happens when users retry.

Marcus does.

// What AI didn't include:  
if (error.code === 'ECONNREFUSED') {  
 // Don't let client retry immediately  
 res.setHeader('Retry-After', '60');  
 return res.status(503).json({  
 error: 'Service temporarily unavailable',  
 retryAfter: 60  
 });  
}
## The Real Difference

AI writes code that:

   Handles the expected input
   Passes tests
   Looks clean
   Works on localhost

Senior engineers write code that:

   Survives production incidents
   Fails gracefully
   Protects downstream services
   Assumes everything will break

AI has never been paged at 3 AM because the database circuit breaker wasn’t implemented.

Marcus has.

That’s the difference.

## What I Learned [...] AI writes code.

Senior engineers write code that survives.

## What Changed For Me

I still use AI.

But now I treat it like a junior developer who’s really fast at typing but has never seen production fail.

AI’s job: Write the first draft  
My job: Add everything AI can’t see

The checklist I use now:

For every AI-generated function:

1.   What happens if external services are down?
2.   What happens if this gets called 1,000x/second?
3.   What happens if the network is slow?
4.   What happens if the data is stale?
5.   What happens if users retry aggressively?
6.   What error messages will help debugging at 3 AM?
7.   What metrics do I need to understand this in production?

AI doesn’t think about these.

I do now. [...] AI doesn’t think about these things.

Because AI has never:

   Debugged a production incident at 2 AM
   Explained to the CEO why the site is down
   Calculated the cost of a database retry storm
   Read postmortems from past failures

AI writes code.

Senior engineers write code that survives reality.

## The Follow-Up Question

Two weeks later, another PR review.

Marcus: “Did you use AI for this?”

Me: “Yes. But I added circuit breaking, error differentiation, and retry headers.”

Marcus: “Good. Now tell me what happens if Redis is down.”

Me: _pulls up code_ “The cache falls back to… oh shit.”

Marcus: “Exactly. Keep thinking.”

## What Tests Can’t Test

My tests said the code was perfect.

results.title: It Is Harder to Review AI Code Than Write It
results.content:
## READING CODE IS ACTUALLY HARDER THAN WRITING IT.

As an open-source maintainer and senior developer, I had to review tons of other people's code, and I learned what Kernighan said the hard way. Reading unfamiliar code is exhausting. You have to reverse-engineer someone else's thought process, figure out why they made certain decisions, and consider edge cases they might have missed.

With my own code, reviewing and adjusting were a no-brainer. I designed it, I wrote it, and the whole mental model was still fresh in my head. Now the code is coming from an LLM and suddenly reviewing "my own code" has become reviewing someone else's code. Except this "someone else" writes faster than I can think and doesn't take lunch breaks. [...] I've been programming since I was ten. When it became a career, I got obsessed with code quality: clean code, design patterns, all that good stuff. My pull requests were polished like nobody's business: well-thought-out logic, proper error handling, comments, tests, documentation. Everything that makes reviewers nod approvingly.

Then, LLMs came along and changed everything. I don't write that much code anymore since AI does it faster. Developer’s work now mainly consists of two parts: explaining to a model what you need, then verifying what it wrote, right? I’ve become more of a code architect and quality inspector rolled into one.
